title: Decomposition and multi-hop retrieval
summary: Decomposition splits a compound question into sub-questions. Multi-hop retrieval chains searches, where each hop depends on what the last one found. Both need stop conditions.
useIf: A question has several parts, or its answer needs a fact that you can only look up after finding another fact.
avoidIf: Questions are single-fact lookups, or you cannot bound hops, tokens and time.

explain.md: One embedding of one question cannot cover 'compare notice periods for contractors and employees in the UK and Germany'. **Decomposition** asks a model to split it into focused sub-questions. If they are independent, run them **in parallel** and merge the evidence. If they depend on each other ('Who manages the owner of service X?'), you need **multi-hop**: retrieve, read, form the next query, retrieve again. IRCoT interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought sentences, so what to retrieve depends on what has been derived. With GPT-3 it improved retrieval by up to 21 points and downstream QA by up to 15 points on four multi-step datasets [[tr3]].

explain.title: Iterative retrieval with stop conditions
explain.alt: A question is planned into sub-queries, retrieved, checked for sufficiency, and either answered or sent around again until a limit is reached.
explain.src:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Plan
  Plan --> Retrieve
  Retrieve --> Check
  Check --> Answer: enough evidence
  Check --> Plan: gap found and budget left
  Check --> Abstain: budget spent
  Answer --> [*]
  Abstain --> [*]

explain.md: **Platform version.** Azure AI Search agentic retrieval plans focused subqueries from the query and chat history, runs all subqueries in parallel and semantically reranks each. At `medium` effort it adds a semantic classifier and one retry with a revised plan [[r5]]. That is a bounded loop. `maxRuntimeInSeconds` has a minimum of 10, a default of 90 and a maximum of 600 (the 600 applies to the Search retrieve request only) [[r38]]. Most of this is preview, as of 2026-10-13 [[r4]].

**Stop conditions are the design.** Combine: a maximum number of hops, a token or time budget, a sufficiency check ('does the evidence answer the question?'), and a no-progress rule (the new query retrieves nothing new). Without them a loop wastes money on unanswerable questions.

explain.title: Errors compound across hops
explain.md: A wrong first-hop answer poisons every later query. Log each sub-question, its evidence and the decision. Prefer parallel decomposition when sub-questions are independent, since serial hops add their latencies.

whereToUse: Comparison questions across entities, regions or time periods
Chain questions such as 'which team owns the service that failed?'
Research assistants that must gather evidence from several documents before answering
Agentic retrieval layers that plan subqueries over multiple knowledge sources

use: Later queries depend on earlier findings
You can bound loops by hops, time and tokens
Single-shot recall is demonstrably low on the multi-part slice
avoid: You cannot afford several model and search calls per question
There is no sufficiency check or stop rule
flips: Sub-questions are independent: run them in parallel rather than serially
Only a slice of traffic is multi-part: route that slice and keep single-shot for the rest
Latency is capped: limit to one plan pass, as the `low` effort does with one planning pass [[r5]]

pitfalls.symptom: A loop keeps searching on an unanswerable question
pitfalls.cause: No hop, token or no-progress limit
pitfalls.fix: Set max hops and a time budget, and abstain when budget is spent

pitfalls.symptom: Final answer ignores one part of the question
pitfalls.cause: The decomposition dropped a sub-question or the merge lost its evidence
pitfalls.fix: Log sub-questions and check that every one has evidence before answering

pitfalls.symptom: Latency is several times higher than single-shot
pitfalls.cause: Independent sub-questions were run in series
pitfalls.fix: Run independent sub-questions in parallel and reserve serial hops for dependent ones

scenarios.title: Compare two jurisdictions
scenarios.situation: An HR assistant gets questions such as 'compare notice periods for contractors and employees in the UK and in Germany'. Single-shot retrieval returns UK employee pages only.
unknowns: What share of traffic is compound?
scenarios.question: How do you retrieve?

options.name: Decompose into four sub-questions, retrieve in parallel, merge and answer with a check that all four have evidence
options.why: The parts are independent, so parallel retrieval keeps latency near one search plus planning.
options.tradeoff: A planning call and four searches per compound question.

options.name: Raise k to 100 on the original query
options.why: One embedding favours the dominant sub-topic, and more chunks flood the context.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a single-topic question with scattered answers.

options.name: Serial multi-hop, one sub-question at a time
options.tradeoff: Latency adds up for no benefit when parts are independent.

flips.if: One answer determines the next query
flips.then: Use iterative hops for that chain.

flips.if: Most questions have one or two facts and latency is tight
flips.then: Skip decomposition and use one hybrid query, reserving decomposition for detected multi-part questions.

scenarios.title: Ownership chain across tickets
scenarios.situation: Engineers ask 'Which on-call group owns the dependency that caused ticket 5512?'. The ticket names a service, the service page names a dependency and the dependency page names a group.
unknowns: What should happen when the chain breaks?
scenarios.question: What stop design do you use?

options.name: Iterative retrieval with a cap of three or four hops, a sufficiency check and abstention on budget exhaustion
options.why: Each hop depends on the last, so serial steps are required, and the caps bound cost.

options.name: Unlimited loop until the model says it is sure
options.why: Unanswerable queries loop forever and spend tokens.
options.tradeoff: Only acceptable with a strict external budget.

options.name: One-shot retrieval with the ticket text
options.tradeoff: Rarely finds the group page, since the answer needs the chain.

flips.if: The ownership data lives in a structured table
flips.then: Use a tool or lookup for the chain instead of text retrieval.

flips.if: Cost no longer matters and recall on deep chains is critical
flips.then: Raise the hop cap modestly, but keep the sufficiency check and a hard ceiling.

options: Who manages the owner of service X?
Compare refund rules in three countries
What did the last answer say?
quiz.explain: The three countries are independent sub-questions. The first is a dependent chain, the third a lookup and the fourth a follow-up.

quiz.q: Select good stop conditions for an iterative retrieval loop.
options: A sufficiency check on the evidence
Keep going until the model is confident
quiz.explain: Hop, budget and sufficiency limits bound the loop. Model confidence alone can run forever on unanswerable questions.

quiz.q: What does Azure's `medium` reasoning effort add compared with `low`?
options: A semantic classifier and one retry with a revised plan
quiz.explain: At `medium` the service adds a semantic classifier and one retry with a revised plan. It is a bounded retry, not an unlimited loop, and reranking stays [[r5]].

flashcards.back: Decomposition splits independent sub-questions that can run in parallel. Multi-hop chains searches where each depends on the last.
It interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought steps so each retrieval depends on what has been derived so far.

flashcards.front: List four stop conditions for a retrieval loop.
flashcards.back: Maximum hops, token or time budget, sufficiency check, and no-new-evidence rule.
